extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners (and patent practitioners interested in §101/abstract-idea analysis)
extracted.subtask_short: identifying abstract ideas in patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether claim limitations recite an abstract idea under Step 2A (Prong One/Two) of the §101 judicial-exception analysis, using enumerated groupings distilled from case law. Applies to examiner claim analysis and related practitioner drafting/response work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office approach: enumerated groupings for identifying abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office uses an approach that distills relevant case law into enumerated groupings of abstract ideas to facilitate examination, shifting examiners' focus from reliance on individual judicial cases to applying a broad body of case law across technologies and claim types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The enumerated groupings are rooted in Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)). This represents a departure from a former case-comparison approach. Examiners should apply these groupings generally rather than relying solely on comparisons to individual cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure to determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should (1) identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recite an abstract idea, and (2) determine whether those limitation(s) fall within at least one of the enumerated abstract-idea groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the identified limitation(s) fall within a grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea in Step 2A Prong One and proceed to Step 2A Prong Two to analyze whether additional claim elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the limitation(s) do not fall within any grouping, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the Step 2A analysis ends (Pathway B), unless another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature) is present. Preferably identify all applicable groupings when a limitation falls within multiple groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping: Mathematical concepts (grouping definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mathematical concepts grouping is defined as mathematical relationships, mathematical formulas or equations, and mathematical calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court and Federal Circuit decisions have repeatedly identified these concepts as abstract ideas (examples: Benson, Flook, Diehr, Bilski, Alice). When determining membership in this grouping, consider whether the claim recites a mathematical concept or merely involves or is based on one. A claim need not use mathematical symbols to recite a mathematical concept; textual descriptions operating on data can serve the same purpose (e.g., 'determining a ratio of A to B').

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical relationship is a relationship between variables or numbers and may be expressed in words or with mathematical symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include relationships such as the Arrhenius equation (reaction rate vs. temperature), conversion between binary-coded decimal and pure binary, relationships between antenna conductor geometry and radio activity, or organizing/manipulating information through mathematical correlations. A claim reciting such relationships, when given its broadest reasonable interpretation, may fall within the mathematical-relationships subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formulas or equations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a numerical formula or equation (or a textual equivalent that replaces a formula) falls within the mathematical concepts grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include explicit formulas (Arrhenius equation, B1 = B0(1.0–F) + PVL(F), F = ma) or textual equivalents such as 'determining a ratio of A to B' or 'calculating the force by multiplying mass and acceleration.' Such recitations are treated as mathematical concepts for eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical calculation is a mathematical operation or act of calculating (e.g., multiplication, exponentiation, statistical resampling) and, when encompassed by the claim's broadest reasonable interpretation, will be considered part of the mathematical concepts grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no single word that must appear; terms like 'determining' or 'performing' may indicate calculations if the claim, in light of the specification, encompasses mathematical operations. Examples include resampled statistical analyses, alarm-limit computations, coordinate conversions, insurance-policy calculations, optimization algorithms, and differences between local and average data values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping: Certain methods of organizing human activity (grouping definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: This grouping describes concepts relating to (a) fundamental economic principles or practices (including hedging, insurance, mitigating risk); (b) commercial or legal interactions (including contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing, sales activities, business relations); and (c) managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (including social activities, teaching, following rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The label 'certain' limits this grouping: not all methods of organizing human activity are abstract ideas (example: a defined set of steps for combining ingredients to create a drug formulation is not a 'certain method of organizing human activity'). The grouping is limited to the enumerated subgroups and should not be expanded except in rare circumstances per MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3). Both single-person activities and multi-person activities may fall within the grouping; the number of people involved is not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental economic practices or principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts relating to the economy and commerce such as hedging, insurance, and mitigating risk are treated as fundamental economic practices within the 'organizing human activity' grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'fundamental' does not necessarily mean 'old'—new methods that embody economic concepts may still qualify (e.g., price optimization, wagering rules). Case examples identifying such practices include Bilski (hedging), Alice (intermediated settlement), Bancorp (insurance-related calculations). Such practices have been held to be unpatentable abstract ideas when claims effectively seek to patent the practice itself and use well-known calculations or steps to implement it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or legal interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: This sub-group includes agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims reciting commercial/legal interactions (e.g., transaction performance guaranties, contractual relationships) can fall within this subgroup. Example: buySAFE v. Google (transaction performance guaranty) identified as a commercial/legal interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing personal behavior or relationships (interactions between people)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts that manage personal behavior, relationships, or interactions between people—such as social activities, teaching, or following rules—may fall within the 'organizing human activity' grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This subgroup covers both interactions between people and some person-computer interactions (e.g., anonymous loan shopping via mobile phone) when the activity itself fits the enumerated subgroups. Determination should focus on the activity type, not the number of participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea grouping: Mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes are concepts performed in the human mind, including observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that recite concepts that can be performed in the human mind may fall into this grouping. Note that a limitation that could be practically performed in the human mind may also overlap with the mathematical concepts grouping (e.g., performing mathematical calculations that could be done mentally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of claims that do not recite abstract ideas (non-limiting hypotheticals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claims do not recite an abstract idea even if they are based on or involve one; such claims are eligible at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting examples provided include: (i) a printer with belt, roller, printhead and ink cartridge; (ii) a washing machine with tub, motor, controller, housing; (iii) an earring sensor for blood glucose measurements with memory; (iv) a BRCA1 sequencing method with PCR and sequencing steps; (v) a method for loading BIOS into a computer by requesting/storing BIOS from remote memory; (vi) a GUI icon-rearrangement method that organizes icons by use and automatically moves most-used icons; (vii) a staged neural-network training method using transformed facial images and non-facial images for second-stage training. These examples illustrate claims that, when read as a whole, do not set forth an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groupings are not mutually exclusive; identify all applicable groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation may fall within more than one abstract-idea grouping or sub-grouping; groupings are not mutually exclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should identify at least one grouping if applicable, but preferably identify all groupings that the limitation falls within to the extent possible (e.g., a claim that performs mathematical calculations that could be done mentally may fall within both the mathematical concepts and mental processes groupings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence of grouping membership and next steps
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim limitation falls within at least one abstract-idea grouping, conclude that the claim recites an abstract idea (Step 2A Prong One) and perform further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether additional elements integrate the abstract idea into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 2A Prong Two examines whether the claim as a whole is directed to the abstract idea or instead integrates it into a practical application (see MPEP § 2106.04(d)). If the Prong Two analysis shows integration into a practical application, the claim may be eligible; otherwise the claim proceeds to the broader Alice/Mayo framework for patent-ineligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: If limitations do not fall within any grouping, claim does not recite an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If the identified limitation(s) do not fall within any of the enumerated groupings, it is reasonable to find the claim does not recite an abstract idea, concluding the abstract-idea eligibility analysis at Step 2A Prong One (Pathway B), unless another judicial exception is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another judicial exception (e.g., law of nature or natural phenomenon) is implicated, follow MPEP §§ 2106.04(b) and 2106.04(c) for Step 2A analysis. Otherwise, the claim is eligible at Step 2A Prong One.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Certain' qualifier: limits expansion of 'organizing human activity' grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'certain' in 'certain methods of organizing human activity' indicates the grouping is limited to the enumerated sub-groupings and should not be expanded beyond them except in rare circumstances (see MPEP § 2106.04(a)(3)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This caution emphasizes that many human-activity-oriented processes are not abstract ideas under this grouping (e.g., a defined set of steps for combining ingredients to create a drug formulation is not within this grouping). Examiners should apply the subgroup definitions and consult § 2106.04(a)(3) for rare expansions.
